candidates.attacker_control: All values in `context.getRequestParameters()` (query string and application/x-www-form-urlencoded POST body) are attacker-controlled on an unauthenticated cross-site POST; a single hidden/auto-submitted form on an attacker page is sufficient to deliver the payload.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified that `escapeHtml` is applied to the action URL and parameter names in the same method and to no other part of the value; verified there is no later encoding step: `DefaultSavedRequestHandler.restore` passes the stored string unchanged to `OkAction` and `JEEHttpActionAdapter` writes it raw; verified the CSRF authorizer does not protect unauthenticated POSTs (DefaultSecurityLogic.java:135-144) so the payload can be planted; verified `getRequestParameters()` returns the raw servlet parameter map (JEEContext.java:53-56). The line fits the repo's 140-char checkstyle limit, i.e. the raw single-line form is a plausible genuine pre-fix version, and adding `escapeHtml(...)` at this line exceeds the limit and would force a re-wrap - consistent with this being the pre-fix state of a later upstream escaping fix, though the upstream fix was not inspectable here.
candidates.impact: Post-authentication cross-site scripting: script execution in the application's origin after the victim logs in, enabling session/CSRF-token theft (including the pac4j CSRF token request attribute/cookie), account actions as the victim, and credential/IdP flow manipulation. High severity if exploited.
candidates.prerequisites: A web application using an IndirectClient with the default `SavedRequestHandler` (`DefaultSavedRequestHandler`, the default in `DefaultSecurityLogic`/`DefaultCallbackLogic`). The CSRF authorizer does not run for unauthenticated requests (authorizers are only evaluated when `profiles` is non-empty, DefaultSecurityLogic.java:135-144), so the forged POST is not blocked. Victim must be unauthenticated (or have an expired profile) and complete the IdP login after the forged POST for the saved content to be replayed; the response is written by the JEE adapter with the container's default content type (typically text/html).
candidates.root_cause: `HttpActionHelper.buildFormPostContent` builds an HTML form by string concatenation. The parameter NAME and the form action URL are passed through `escapeHtml(...)`, but the parameter VALUE is concatenated raw: `... + "\" value=\"" + values[0] + "\" />\n"` (HttpActionHelper.java:86). `escapeHtml` (lines 98-100) escapes `&`, `<` and `"`, so the missing call allows an attacker-controlled value containing `"` and `<script>`/event handlers to break out of the quoted attribute and inject markup. The generated content is not re-encoded anywhere downstream.
candidates.title: Reflected/stored XSS via unescaped request-parameter values in HttpActionHelper.buildFormPostContent (saved request handling)
candidates.trace:
1) Attacker page auto-submits POST /protected with e.g. param x=`\"><script>...<\/script>`; victim has no pac4j profile.
2) DefaultSecurityLogic.perform -> no profiles -> startAuthentication -> saveRequestedUrl -> DefaultSavedRequestHandler.save; because the request is a POST, HttpActionHelper.buildFormPostContent is called and the generated HTML (with the raw value) is stored as an OkAction under Pac4jConstants.REQUESTED_URL (DefaultSavedRequestHandler.java:25-31).
3) Victim authenticates via the indirect client; DefaultCallbackLogic.redirectToOriginallyRequestedUrl -> DefaultSavedRequestHandler.restore returns OkAction with the stored content (DefaultSavedRequestHandler.java:56-61).
4) JEEHttpActionAdapter.adapt writes `content` to `response.getWriter()` (JEEHttpActionAdapter.java:43-53), so the injected script executes in the application origin with the victim's authenticated session.
candidates.unverified: No runtime execution or test run was performed, so the XSS is not runtime-confirmed: the exact content type used by the container for the generated response and the victim-login interaction were reasoned from source only. The application must use the default saved-request mechanism and an IndirectClient for the flow to apply; an app that overrides SavedRequestHandler/CallbackLogic or only uses direct clients is not affected.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

coverage_summary: Read-level review of the visible snapshot: pac4j-core engine/authorizer/matcher/serializer/saved-request code, pac4j-jee adapter/session/context, pac4j-jwt config, pac4j-oauth/oidc creators and redirect builders, parts of pac4j-saml validators/decoders, pac4j-cas, pac4j-http direct clients, profile services (SQL/LDAP) and configuration builders. The source scope excludes 53 files by 'sensitive name or path' filters (the entire org.pac4j.*.credentials.* packages, including credential extractors/authenticators where OAuth state/nonce verification and password checks live), so those trust-boundary components could not be inspected. No test sources are present in the snapshot. The P1 relation index is partial, syntax-only, has no data-flow/semantic resolution, and contains no relation facts for the saved-request/CSRF code; all candidate traces were verified directly against source text, and no code was executed.
limitations: No runtime, test, or scanner execution: the XSS candidate is a source-level lead, not a confirmed exploit; real behavior depends on the container's default response content type and on the victim completing the login flow.

Fixed-upstream comparison was impossible without external access, so it cannot be excluded that the unescaped value and the missing `//` logout check are long-standing upstream code rather than the benchmark's introduced defect; the choice between them is based on source evidence and reachability reasoning.
Credential/authenticator/extractor classes (paths matching the sensitive-name filter, including OAuth/OIDC state and nonce validation code) were not visible, so those trust boundaries are unreviewed.

Large SAML and OIDC validation files were reviewed only selectively (signature, audience, replay, InResponseTo, authn-instant checks were spot-checked), so an additional issue there cannot be excluded.
The P1 index omits files and lacks flow/semantic resolution; no index edge was treated as proof of reachability.

rejected_leads.lead: Open redirect in DefaultLogoutLogic: `url` request parameter matching the default pattern `/.*` (Pac4jConstants.java:59) still accepts protocol-relative URLs such as `//evil.com`, and the value is put into the raw Location header (JEEHttpActionAdapter.java:39-41), while the docs state that only relative URLs are allowed (documentation/docs/logout-endpoint.md:38).
rejected_leads.reason: Real-looking CWE-601 weakness and still the second-strongest lead, but I could not confirm it fits this snapshot better than the XSS: the code is equally consistent with a later upstream fix (there is no in-repo evidence of the intended `//` check and no runtime confirmation that the browser/container treats the Location value as protocol-relative), so it was kept as a rejected/unconfirmed lead to respect the one-candidate cap.

rejected_leads.lead: CsrfAuthorizer.hashEquals compares `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` (CsrfAuthorizer.java:80-85) and an absent/empty session PREVIOUS_CSRF_TOKEN becomes "", so an empty submitted token can satisfy `hashEquals("", "")`.
rejected_leads.reason: Tracing the default flow shows the csrfToken matcher runs before the authorizer in DefaultSecurityLogic (DefaultSecurityLogic.java:90 then 135-138) and regenerates the token (DefaultMatchingChecker.computeDefaultMatchers + DefaultCsrfTokenGenerator.get), so PREVIOUS is normally non-empty at check time; a practical bypass therefore needs an unusual configuration where tokens are generated without the matcher running on the checked request. Exploitation also needs knowledge of the 32-bit token hash for collision; reachability/impact could not be established from source, so it is not submitted as the candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: LdapProfileService builds the search filter by string concatenation (`key + "=" + value`, LdapProfileService.java:146-151) and DbProfileService interpolates attribute names into SQL (DbProfileService.java:131-136).
rejected_leads.reason: Both use internally chosen keys/attributes and bound values for the attacker-relevant path (`validate` uses LDAP bind, SQL uses bind parameters); no attacker-controlled value reaches the interpolated position in the paths reviewed, so this is at most a hardening/design concern.

rejected_leads.lead: JavaSerializer deserialization whitelist includes broad packages (java., org.joda., com.nimbusds., net.minidev.json., ...) and BasicUserProfile.readExternal reads nested objects (BasicUserProfile.java:471-481).
rejected_leads.reason: This is the upstream-designed restricted ObjectInputStream behavior and the serializer is used for server-side profile stores, not directly on request data in the reviewed code; no concrete gadget chain or attacker-controlled deserialization entry point was established.

summary: Reviewed the pac4j 5.2.0-SNAPSHOT source tree (523 visible Java files; index coverage partial and syntax-only). The strongest evidence-supported issue is an HTML-injection/XSS sink in the saved-request ("form post") mechanism: `HttpActionHelper.buildFormPostContent` interpolates raw request-parameter values into an HTML attribute that pac4j later writes verbatim into the response body, while the sibling interpolations (form action URL and parameter names) are passed through `escapeHtml`. An unauthenticated attacker can make the victim POST attacker-controlled values to a protected URL; pac4j stores the generated HTML in the session and returns it after login, executing script in the application origin. Two other leads (protocol-relative open redirect in `DefaultLogoutLogic`, and CSRF token comparison by `String.hashCode` with an empty-previous-token match in `CsrfAuthorizer`) were checked and are reported only as rejected/unconfirmed leads, not as additional candidates.
